articles.title: Experts say ‘trusted messengers’ critical as Amish grapple with measles outbreak
articles.summary_snippet: Unfolding crisis shows importance of ‘human connections’ over the long term – especially in under-vaccinated areas Tristan Sharratt, a family nurse practitioner and public health researcher, began serving an Amish community in central New York almost inadvertently. A friend told an Amish neighbor that Sharratt was accepting new patients and was a good, solid guy. Word spread quickly, and now Sharratt sees many members of the community, which numbers in the hundreds. He is what is called a “trusted messenger” – someone who understands a community and has earned their respect. Other trusted messengers can be neighbors, co-workers, customers, midwives, or people who work as long-distance drivers for the Amish. Connecting with such people will be crucial for ending the measles outbreak and preventing future crises. Continue reading...

articles.summary_snippet: For decades, it served pancakes, hash browns and steaks to hungry Angelenos. Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad. For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. They were all killed by Soviet forces after the USSR’s invasion of Estonia in 1940. For 51 years, Estonia was occupied by its imperial neighbour; for the past 25 years it has lived independently in its shadow. articles.title: New Orleans Catholic clergy abuse survivors begin receiving payments from $305m bankruptcy settlement
articles.summary_snippet: Arrival of payments in contentious legal saga that began in 2020 is ‘a weight off my shoulders’, one survivor said Hundreds of clergy sexual abuse survivors have received more than half of the $305m bankruptcy settlement that the archdiocese of New Orleans reached with them last year, a milestone that marks the beginning of the end of a years-long legal saga. The trustee overseeing the settlement fund, Don Massey, confirmed on Friday that $180m had been distributed to 450 of about 740 survivors, either directly or through their lawyers if they retained legal representation. Massey said he and his staff are working hard to get payments in the rest of the survivors’ hands by the end of the year but are still waiting on hundreds of distribution forms from survivors and their lawyers. articles.summary_snippet: Red Command (Comando Vermelho) The Red Command (Comando Vermelho – CV) is Brazil’s oldest criminal group. Created in a Rio de Janeiro prison in the 1970s as a self-protection group for prisoners, it started out with low-level crimes like muggings and bank robberies. But in the 1980s, the group moved into the cocaine trade, working with Colombian drug cartels and taking on a social leadership role in many of Rio’s marginalized neighborhoods. articles.summary_snippet: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. articles.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
articles.summary_snippet: Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none. The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences. Continue reading...

articles.title: NFL legend John Madden’s unlikely, unfiltered brilliance: ‘Coach was indeed animated’
articles.summary_snippet: With the release of a new David O Russell biopic about the coach turned commentator turned gaming icon, those who knew him best remember his singular career Wearing his Oakland Raiders uniform and helmet, and gripping an orange traffic cone like a lance, Ted Hendricks rode into the training session on a roan horse and stopped at the 50-yard line. Some American football coaches might have reacted to the stunt with fury. But John Madden was unfazed. “We needed some relief from the intense grind,” recalls Hendricks, 79, who had borrowed the horse from a nearby stable. “It was a spur of the moment idea, but put a smile on everyone’s face. All Coach said once I dismounted was, ‘All right guys, Ted’s here, let’s get started.’ But I know he got a kick out of it too – just from the look on his face and the comments he made later in interviews.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers
articles.summary_snippet: Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations. Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate. Continue reading...
